$comment: Read from monday's own introspection schema (GET /v2/get_schema, served unauthenticated), not from docs prose. create_item(board_id: ID!, item_name: String!, column_values: JSON, group_id: String, ...) -> Item.
title: monday.com item
description: Create an item on a monday.com board.
$idempotencyComment: monday offers no idempotency key on create_item -- there is no header and no argument for one in the schema. So this is honestly `unsafe-to-replay` with no way to make it safe, and saying so is better than implying a guarantee the API cannot give. A retried durable run creates a SECOND item.

request.$pathComment: Every monday operation is POST /v2. The path says nothing about what is being called -- the document does -- which is the whole reason `graphql` is an encoding rather than a spelling of `json`.

config.label: Board ID
config.description: The numeric id in the board URL: monday.com/boards/1234567890.
config.$comment: ID! in the schema. monday's ID accepts a numeric string, and sending it as a string avoids the precision loss a large board id would suffer as a JSON number.

config.label: Item name
config.description: What the item is called on the board.

config.label: Group ID
config.description: Which group on the board to create it in. Left empty, monday uses the board's default group.

config.label: Column values
config.description: Column id to value, e.g. status -> Done. Which values a column accepts depends on its type.

send.$comment: json, NOT object. monday's `JSON` scalar is documented in its own schema as `A JSON formatted string` -- so this variable carries a STRING containing JSON, not a map. Sending the map would put an object where monday expects text, and it rejects it. This is the mirror of the trap Telegram forced `encoding: object` in for, and the two are one keystroke apart.

outputShape.description: The item's name as monday stored it.
Link to the item on the board.

$outputComment: Rooted at `data.create_item` because that is where GraphQL puts it -- the response envelope is `{data: {<field>: ...}}` and the field is named by the document. Flattening it here would make an author who wires {{ $json.data.create_item.id }} against the faker find a different path when a real item arrives.

contract.$comment: The surface this action USES, which is what drift-check stores and diffs. For a GraphQL provider these are the mutation's ARGUMENT names and the selected FIELD names -- not URL paths, because there is only one path and it says nothing.
